reference.source: Murray and Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
clinicalPearls: Plastic bronchitis is characterised by the formation of large, cohesive, branching airway casts that take the shape of the bronchial tree and are expectorated or removed bronchoscopically.
Expectoration of a rubbery, branching cast is virtually diagnostic; patients may describe coughing up a 'tree-shaped' or 'model' of their airways.
In children it is classically associated with congenital heart disease following Fontan-type palliation, where abnormal lymphatic flow drives cast formation.
Other associations include asthma and allergic bronchopulmonary disease, sickle cell acute chest syndrome, and lymphatic disorders or thoracic duct abnormalities.
Casts are broadly divided into lymphatic/acellular fibrin-rich types (often in cardiac and lymphatic disease) and inflammatory eosinophil- or mucin-rich types (often in asthma and allergic disease).
Acute large-cast impaction can cause lobar or whole-lung collapse and life-threatening airway obstruction, sometimes with sudden severe respiratory distress.
Bronchoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic, allowing extraction of casts and sampling to characterise their composition.
In lymphatic disease, cross-sectional lymphatic imaging can identify abnormal pulmonary lymphatic flow amenable to lymphatic embolisation or surgical correction.
reference.pathophysiology: Plastic bronchitis involves the accumulation and consolidation of material within the airways into firm, cohesive casts that replicate the branching bronchial anatomy. In lymphatic-type disease, often after Fontan palliation of single-ventricle physiology, chronically elevated systemic venous and lymphatic pressures cause abnormal pulmonary lymphatic networks to leak protein-rich, fibrin-laden lymph into the airways, which coagulates into acellular fibrinous casts. In inflammatory-type disease, airway inflammation — as in asthma, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis or the acute chest syndrome of sickle cell disease — generates mucin, fibrin and cellular exudate (frequently eosinophil-rich) that inspissates into casts. Once formed, a cast behaves as an obstructing intraluminal plug: it impairs ventilation of the subtended lung, promotes atelectasis and post-obstructive infection, and, if it dislodges into a central airway, can cause acute critical obstruction. The composition of the cast reflects the underlying mechanism and guides directed therapy.
additionalDifferentials: mucoid impaction in allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis
aspirated foreign body causing lobar collapse
thick tenacious secretions in cystic fibrosis or severe asthma
endobronchial tumour or broncholith with obstruction
pulmonary haemorrhage with organised clot cast
diphtheritic or other pseudomembranous airway disease
acute chest syndrome of sickle cell disease
additionalInvestigations: flexible or rigid bronchoscopy for cast extraction and airway inspection
histopathological analysis of the cast to classify lymphatic versus inflammatory type
chest CT to assess atelectasis, bronchiectasis and mediastinal or lymphatic abnormality
dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance lymphangiography or intranodal lymphangiography
echocardiography and assessment of Fontan haemodynamics in relevant patients
evaluation for asthma and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis where inflammatory casts are found
haemoglobinopathy screening where sickle cell disease is suspected
redFlags: acute severe respiratory distress from central cast impaction
lobar or whole-lung collapse on imaging
hypoxaemia or asphyxiation risk requiring urgent airway clearance
recurrent casts in a Fontan patient indicating protein-losing lymphatic complications
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the underlying cause: inflammatory casts related to asthma or allergic disease often respond to control of airway inflammation, whereas Fontan-associated lymphatic plastic bronchitis is more refractory, though lymphatic imaging and targeted embolisation have substantially improved outcomes in selected patients.
pitfalls: Failing to retrieve and analyse the cast, thereby missing the distinction between lymphatic and inflammatory types that dictates treatment.
Treating recurrent Fontan-associated casts purely as mucus without investigating pulmonary lymphatic flow.
Underestimating the risk of acute asphyxiation from a mobile central cast.
Overlooking allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis or poorly controlled asthma as a driver of inflammatory casts.
Relying on mucolytics or physiotherapy alone in refractory disease without escalating to bronchoscopy or lymphatic intervention.

management: Remove obstructing casts by flexible or rigid bronchoscopy to relieve airway obstruction and re-expand collapsed lung
For Fontan-associated lymphatic disease, optimise Fontan haemodynamics and pursue lymphatic imaging with percutaneous lymphatic or thoracic duct embolisation to interrupt abnormal lymph leakage
Institute a low-fat, medium-chain-triglyceride diet, and consider octreotide, to reduce lymphatic output in lymphatic-type casts
Treat inflammatory-type disease by controlling airway inflammation with inhaled corticosteroids and bronchodilators and by managing underlying asthma or allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis
Support cast clearance with airway clearance physiotherapy, mucolytics, and nebulised fibrinolytics such as tissue plasminogen activator or DNase
Treat acute large-cast impaction as an emergency with airway stabilisation and urgent therapeutic bronchoscopy
Coordinate care across respiratory, cardiology and interventional radiology teams and escalate for refractory or life-threatening obstruction
